newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's top paper makers see profits slip.
newsitem.headline: Japan's top paper makers see profits slip.

text.p: Higher costs resulting from the weaker yen and cuts in production shaved half-year profits at Japan's top paper manufacturers, which reported uninspiring earnings on Friday.
Unlike major Japanese exporters, which benefit from a fall in the yen, Japan's paper industry has been hurt by the trend as it raises the cost of raw materials.
The bottom line was also damaged by a need to rein in production because of high inventories, which meant fewer economies of scale and increased manufacturing costs.
"The weaker trend of the yen and output adjustments pushed up our production costs," said a Nippon Paper Industries Co Ltd spokesman, adding that a quick recovery was unlikely.

Nippon Paper, Japan's second-largest paper and pulp manufacturer, announced that its parent current profit in the April-September period fell 9.6 percent from the same period a year ago to 18.57 billion yen ($164 million). Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses made on securities investments and other non-operating activities.

Japan's newest and biggest paper and pulp maker, Oji Paper Co Ltd, said it also suffered a fall in profits in the six months to September 30. Oji Paper was born earlier this month through a merger between New Oji Paper Co Ltd and Honshu Paper Co Ltd.

Oji said although Honshu Paper's half-year parent current profit rose two percent from the year-ago period, the combined parent current profit was lower because New Oji's parent current profit fell 2.2 percent.
"We implemented cost-cutting steps...but still could not avoid an increase in costs due to factors like the fall in the yen," Oji Paper said in a statement.
The yen has dropped about 13 percent over the past year.

The manufacturers import materials such as wood chips so a weaker yen means higher costs. The bulk of the paper makers' business is in Japan, with only a small part of their production going for export.
The paper makers also cut production of some products in order to reduce inventories, the Nippon Paper spokesman said, and the smaller output meant relatively larger costs.

The paper and pulp industry has suffered huge stockpiles of leftover paper, as demand for computer-related instruction manuals, books and magazines has been less robust than last year, industry analysts said.
But demand for catalogues and flyers and for newsprint rose in the April-September period and all three firms managed to slightly increase sales in the half-year period.
Both Oji Paper and Nippon Paper were downbeat about the earnings outlook for the full year to March 31.

"For the second half of the 1996/97 business year, the supply-demand situation is unclear and there are other worrisome factors like cost increases due to the weaker yen," Nippon Paper said in a statement.
Nippon Paper expects a parent current profit of 41 billion yen ($362 million) for the full 1996/97 business year against 44.02 billion yen ($389 million) the previous year.

Oji Paper expects a parent current profit of 48 billion yen ($424 million) in 1996/97. New Oji posted a parent current profit of 48.07 billion yen ($425 million) in 1995/96 while Honshu Paper posted a parent current profit of 9.80 billion yen ($86.7 million).
